Seminar Title:

Aerosol Effects on Raindrop Size Distribution: Insights from Observations and High-Resolution Numerical Simulations Using the WRF Model

Seminar Type:

Synopsis Seminar

Department:

Earth and Atmospheric Sciences

Speaker Name:

Dola Tharun ( Rollno : 521er1009)

Speaker Type:

Student

Venue:

ER303, Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences

Date and Time:

10 Aug 2026 16:30

Contact:

Bhishma Tyagi

Abstract:

The raindrop size distribution (DSD) affects rainfall intensity, flash floods, soil erosion, agriculture, cloud lifetime, and climate feedback. It has been observed that one of the key drivers of DSD variability is aerosol, which acts as Cloud Condensation Nuclei (CCN). The high concentration of CCN increases the droplet number concentration, suppresses collision-coalescence, reduces the mass-weighted mean diameter (Dm), and makes raindrops narrower in polluted environments. The CCN in convective systems can invigorates updrafts and produces broader DSD through ice-phase processes. Ground-based disdrometers, ground-based weather radars, and the airborne Global Precipitation Measurement Dual-frequency precipitation radar (GPM-DPR) are some of the sources that provide DSD variables. DSD variables vary with meteorological parameters such as temperature, relative humidity, sensible heat flux, latent heat flux, geography, rainfall type (convective, stratiform, mixed convective and stratiform), and multiscale weather phenomena. The current thesis aims to understand the sensitivity of DSD variables to aerosols and urbanisation in micro-, meso-, and synoptic-scale weather phenomena using ground-based observations (disdrometer, X-band radar), GPM-DPR, and numerical modelling during pre-monsoon, monsoon, and post-monsoon rainfall.

In the first objective, pre-monsoon and monsoon rainfall days have been divided into polluted (PD) and non-polluted (NPD) days based on the Ari Quality Index (AQI). The one-minute disdrometer data have been used to examine DSD variability from 2018 to 2021. Using empirical formulas, the responses of DSD variables to aerosols have been checked. In both seasons, the PD showed a lower concentration of larger raindrops and a higher concentration of smaller droplets. To understand the differences in DSD between PD and NPD, the probability distribution functions (PDFs) for rain integral parameters (Rain Rate, radar reflectivity, mass-weighted mean diameter, and normalised intercept parameter) have been examined. The PDF of rain integral parameters showed a significant difference between PD and NPD. Empirical relations such as Z-R, Dm-R, and Nw-R have been examined to understand changes in microphysical characteristics during PD and NPD. All empirical relations indicated that PD has a lower concentration of larger droplets, whereas NPD has a higher concentration of smaller droplets. The second objective attempted to understand the changes in microphysical properties during PD and NPD above and below the melting layer. The contoured frequency-by-altitude diagram (CFAD) has been used to understand the vertical profiles of Z, Dm, and Nw during PD and NPD over four major Eastern Indian cities (Kolkata, Rourkela, Ranchi, and Bhubaneswar). The CFADs of Z, Dm of Kolkata, Rourkela, and Ranchi showed a broad distribution in PD and a narrow distribution in NPD, whereas in Bhubaneswar, the opposite was observed. The distribution of CFAD for Z, Dm, and Nw shows that Kolkata, Rourkela, and Ranchi exhibit higher (lower) reflectivity and higher (lower) Dm, with lower concentration in PD (NPD). The CFAD of Bhubaneswar shows contrasting results, with a higher concentration of larger drops in NPD compared with PD.

Furthermore, the microphysical processes have been examined in PD and NPD NPD in all the four cities by scrutinizing the two-dimensional distribution pattern of the and of the &DeltaZe &nbspand &DeltaDm &nbsp(&DeltaZe=&DeltaZe2 km-Ze3 km &DeltaDm= Dm2 km- Dm3 km ). The &DeltaZe &nbspand &DeltaDm reveals that the dominant microphysical process shifts from coalescence in NPD to breakup in and evaporation in PD for inland cities whereas the coastal city showed balanced coalescence process in both PD and NPD.

The third objective concerns the comparison of simulated DSD variables with X-band radar-measured dual-polarisation variables during a synoptic-scale weather phenomenon. For this objective, the NIVAR cyclone has been considered. The sensitivity experiments have been conducted with the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model using two cloud microphysics schemes (CMP) (Thompson and Morrison) with and without aerosol-cloud feedback. Polarimetric radar observations reveal a clear transition from stratiform-dominated in the initial hours of the cyclone with small drops and moderate horizontal reflectivity (ZH), low differential reflectivity (ZDR), and low specific differential phase (KDP), to intense convective in the developing and mature stage of the cyclone, with large ZH, high ZDR, low KDP, and large mean diameter (Dm), indicating strong size sorting and efficient warm-rain processes. The Thompson scheme consistently overestimates ZH, ZDR, KDP, and Dm in the developing and mature stages, reflecting overly strong convection and excessive drop growth. The Morrison-based simulations underestimated the polarimetric radar variables compared with the Thompson-based schemes.
